r0.why: No charge, slightly heavier than proton [1], in nuclei with similar number of protons [3], three quarks [9], nuclear physics [8].

r1.why: Isotopes differ only in neutron number [4]; Latin neuter root plus Greek -on as in electron/proton [16].

r2.why: Free neutron decay to p, e, antineutrino, ~15 min mean lifetime [10]; fission/fusion [5]; dedicated sources [12]; natural background from cosmic rays and spontaneously fissionable crust elements [14].

r3.why: 1911 model [17], 1920 neutral proton-electron particle [18], 1920s nuclear electrons [22], 1928 clash with quantum theory [23], spin inconsistency [26].

r4.why: Bothe/Becker 1931 [30-31], Joliot-Curies following year paraffin [32], Chadwick doubted and showed uncharged proton-mass particles [33-34], matched hypothesis [35], 1935 Nobel [36].

r5.why: Fermi 1934 [41], December 1938 fission by Hahn/Meitner/Strassmann [43], led to power and bomb by end of WWII [45], essential to nuclear power [11].

r6.why: Stellar nucleosynthesis via fission/fusion/capture [6], neutron stars at nuclear density with more than solar mass [7], indirect ionization biological hazard depending on dose [13].
